response.content:
# Consistency Models and Failure Modes in Distributed Systems

## 1. Consistency Models

Consistency models specify a contract between a distributed storage or computation system and its clients: given a set of concurrent operations, which orderings and visibility guarantees are legal. Models differ chiefly along two axes — the strength of the ordering imposed on operations across different processes/objects, and whether that ordering must respect real (wall-clock) time.

### 1.1 Linearizability

Linearizability (also called atomic consistency or strong consistency in the single-object, single-operation sense) is the strongest consistency model commonly implemented in real systems. It requires that:

- Every operation (read or write) on a single object appears to take effect instantaneously at some point between its invocation and its response (the atomicity/single-operation property).
- All operations are totally ordered, and this total order is consistent with real time: if operation A completes (returns) before operation B is invoked (in real/wall-clock time), then A must appear before B in the order observed by every process.
- All processes agree on this single total order (there is one global sequence of operations on the object).

Formally, for every execution there must exist a linearization point for each operation, and the resulting sequential history must be legal (consistent with the object's sequential specification) and must respect the real-time precedence order of non-overlapping operations. Linearizability composes: a system built from linearizable objects is itself linearizable, which makes it attractive as a building block. It is inherently a single-object consistency model — it says nothing directly about the ordering of operations across multiple distinct objects, which is where strict serializability (below) diverges.

### 1.2 Sequential Consistency

Sequential consistency, introduced by Lamport in the context of shared-memory multiprocessors, requires that:

- There exists some total order of all operations from all processes.
- This total order is consistent with each individual process's program order (the order in which that process issued its own operations).
- All processes observe the same total order.

Critically, sequential consistency drops the real-time constraint of linearizability: the total order need not respect the actual invocation/response timing between different processes. An operation that completed before another began (in real time) may legally appear after it in the agreed total order, as long as per-process program order is preserved. This makes sequential consistency strictly weaker than linearizability but still strong enough to prevent many anomalies; it is not composable in the same way linearizability is, because combining sequentially consistent components does not guarantee the composite system is sequentially consistent.

### 1.3 Causal Consistency

Causal consistency weakens the total order requirement to a partial order based on Lamport's happens-before relation. Operation A happens-before operation B if:

- A and B are issued by the same process and A precedes B in program order, or
- A is a write and B is a read that observes A's value (read-from relation), or
- The relation is transitively closed over the above.

Causal consistency requires that all processes observe causally related operations in the same relative order; operations that are concurrent (unrelated by happens-before) may be observed in different orders by different processes. This is typically implemented using vector clocks (one logical clock entry per process/replica), which allow a system to determine whether two events are causally ordered or concurrent by comparing component-wise clock values. Causal consistency is the strongest model that remains available under network partitions in the sense characterized by later CAP-related work (it does not require synchronous coordination between partitions for concurrent, non-causally-related operations).

### 1.4 Eventual Consistency and Session Guarantees

Eventual consistency is a liveness-oriented guarantee rather than a safety-oriented ordering guarantee: it states only that if no new updates are made to a given object, all replicas will eventually converge to the same value. It makes no promises about intermediate states, ordering, or how long convergence takes. Because the guarantee is so weak, practical systems often layer session guarantees on top of eventual consistency to give individual clients a more coherent view:

- Read-your-writes (RYW): a process that writes a value will subsequently observe that write (or a later one) in its own reads; it will never read a value older than its own prior write.
- Monotonic reads: if a process reads a value of an object, any subsequent read by that process will return that value or a more recent one — reads never go "backward" in time for a single client.
- Monotonic writes: writes by a single process are applied in the order they were issued; a replica never applies a process's writes out of order.
- Writes-follow-reads (session causality): if a process reads a value and then issues a write, that write is ordered after (and causally dependent upon) any writes that produced the value it read, so the write is propagated to other replicas only after those prior writes.

These session guarantees are orthogonal, composable building blocks; many systems (e.g., Dynamo-style stores) offer some subset of them to approximate stronger semantics without full linearizability.

### 1.5 Serializability vs. Strict Serializability vs. Linearizability

These three terms are frequently conflated and need precise separation:

- Serializability is a transactional isolation guarantee: it states that the concurrent execution of a set of transactions is equivalent to some serial (one-at-a-time) execution of those same transactions. It says nothing about which serial order is chosen relative to real time, and nothing about single-object operation semantics outside of transactions.
- Strict serializability adds the real-time constraint to serializability: the equivalent serial order of transactions must also respect real-time precedence — if transaction T1 commits before T2 begins, T1 must precede T2 in the serial order.
- Linearizability is the single-object, single-operation analogue — it is essentially strict serializability restricted to transactions that each consist of a single operation on a single object. Strict serializability is linearizability generalized to multi-object, multi-operation transactions.

Thus the strength ordering is: strict serializability is strictly stronger than both plain serializability (it adds real-time ordering) and than linearizability generalized naively (it handles multi-object transactions, which linearizability alone does not address). Systems can be serializable without being linearizable (e.g., a system that reorders non-overlapping transactions as long as some serial equivalent exists), and can be linearizable on individual objects without offering any cross-object transactional isolation.

### 1.6 PRAM Consistency

Pipelined Random Access Memory (PRAM) consistency, sometimes called FIFO consistency, is weaker than causal consistency. It requires only that writes issued by a single process are seen by all other processes in the order they were issued (program order is preserved per-writer), but it imposes no ordering constraint on writes from different processes relative to one another, and does not require the read-from causal relation that causal consistency enforces. It is effectively "monotonic writes" elevated to a system-wide model rather than a per-session guarantee.

### 1.7 CAP Theorem

The CAP theorem, as rigorously formalized by Gilbert and Lynch (2002) building on Brewer's conjecture, concerns a distributed data store under a network partition and defines:

- Consistency (C): here specifically meaning atomic/linearizable consistency — every read receives the most recent write or an error.
- Availability (A): every request received by a non-failing node must result in a response (not an error, and not an indefinite wait).
- Partition tolerance (P): the system continues to operate despite an arbitrary number of messages being dropped or delayed by the network between nodes.

Gilbert and Lynch's theorem states precisely: it is impossible for an asynchronous distributed system to simultaneously guarantee linearizable consistency and availability in the presence of a network partition. The theorem is a statement about the specific moment a partition exists, not a general "pick two of three" trade-off to be applied at all times — this is the most common misinterpretation. In practice, since partitions can and do occur, the real design choice a system makes is: when a partition occurs, do you sacrifice consistency (remain available but risk returning stale or divergent data, i.e., an AP system) or sacrifice availability (remain consistent but refuse/block requests on the minority or isolated side, i.e., a CP system)? "Choosing CA" is not a meaningful option for a system that must tolerate partitions, since partitions are a property of the network, not a choice of the system; a system that assumes no partitions will occur is not partition-tolerant by definition, and in practice all systems spanning more than one network segment must contend with partition tolerance. Another common misreading treats C, A, and P as continuously tunable independent dials at all times, when the theorem's force applies specifically during partition events.

### 1.8 PACELC

PACELC, introduced by Daniel Abadi, refines CAP by observing that CAP only describes behavior during a Partition (PAC: under partition, choose Availability or Consistency), but says nothing about system behavior during normal operation when no partition exists. PACELC adds: Else, i.e. in the absence of a partition, there is still a trade-off between Latency and Consistency (EL C) — a system can choose to replicate synchronously (favoring consistency, at the cost of higher latency) or asynchronously (favoring low latency, at the cost of potential inconsistency), even when the network is healthy. This yields a more complete taxonomy, e.g., Dynamo-style systems are typically classified PA/EL (available under partition, low-latency/weakly-consistent otherwise), while systems like traditional synchronously-replicated relational databases are PC/EC.

---

## 2. Failure Modes

Failure modes characterize the ways in which processes, links, or entire subsystems can deviate from correct behavior. The choice of failure model determines which fault-tolerance algorithms are applicable and what resilience bounds (e.g., quorum sizes) are required.

### 2.1 Crash-Stop (Fail-Stop) Failures

In the crash-stop (fail-stop) model, a process executes correctly according to its specification until it fails, at which point it halts permanently and performs no further actions — it does not send further messages, does not corrupt state, and (in the idealized fail-stop variant) its failure is reliably detectable by other processes. This is the weakest and most benign failure assumption and underlies many classical consensus and replication protocols (e.g., basic Paxos is typically described under crash-stop/crash-recovery assumptions).

### 2.2 Crash-Recovery Failures

The crash-recovery model relaxes crash-stop by allowing a process to halt and later resume execution, possibly losing its volatile (in-memory) state but retaining any state it had durably persisted (e.g., to stable storage) before crashing. Protocols designed for crash-recovery must account for a process rejoining mid-protocol with partial amnesia, which requires careful use of persistent logs, write-ahead logging, and idempotent or replay-safe message handling to avoid violating safety properties on recovery.

### 2.3 Omission Failures

Omission failures occur when a process fails to send or receive a message that it was supposed to send or receive, while otherwise continuing to execute correctly:

- Send-omission: the process's internal state is updated as though a message were sent, but the message never actually leaves the process (e.g., due to a buffer failure or crashed outgoing network stack).
- Receive-omission: a message is correctly delivered to the process's incoming buffer but the process fails to process it (e.g., due to a full receive buffer or a bug in message handling).

Omission failures are a strictly larger failure class than crash-stop, since a crashed process can be viewed as one that omits all sends and receives from the point of failure onward.

### 2.4 Timing Failures

Timing failures (also called performance failures) occur in systems with timing assumptions — generally synchronous or partially synchronous systems — when a process's response, or a message's delivery, falls outside an expected time bound, even though the content of the response/message is correct. In partially synchronous systems (where timing bounds exist but are unknown or hold only after some unknown stabilization time, per Dwork, Lynch, and Stockmeyer), timing failures manifest as a process or link that is slow rather than crashed, which complicates failure detection because slowness is indistinguishable, from the outside, from a crash until some timeout threshold is exceeded. This is also the formal basis of the gray failure / fail-slow phenomenon discussed below.

### 2.5 Byzantine Failures

Byzantine failures represent the most general and severe failure class: a faulty process may exhibit arbitrary behavior, including sending conflicting, contradictory, or deliberately malicious messages to different peers, selectively omitting messages, or colluding with other faulty processes, with no restriction on behavior beyond what the network/cryptographic model prevents. This model, originating from Lamport, Shostak, and Pease's "Byzantine Generals" formulation, is the appropriate model for adversarial settings (e.g., permissionless blockchains, systems with untrusted or compromised nodes) and for providing the strongest possible fault-tolerance guarantees.

Byzantine fault tolerance (BFT) protocols that must achieve consensus or agreement in the presence of Byzantine actors generally require at least 3f+1 total nodes to tolerate f Byzantine faults (equivalently, fewer than one-third of nodes may be faulty), because a two-thirds supermajority is the minimum needed to guarantee that any quorum intersection among honest nodes is large enough to prevent the faulty minority from causing disagreement or forging a false quorum. This bound (n ≥ 3f+1) holds for asynchronous or partially synchronous BFT consensus without additional cryptographic assumptions like trusted hardware or digital signatures that can sometimes relax the bound in restricted models. Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance (PBFT), introduced by Castro and Liskov, is the canonical state-machine-replication protocol achieving BFT consensus in a partially synchronous network using this 3f+1 bound, via a three-phase (pre-prepare, prepare, commit) message pattern and a rotating primary (view-based leader election with view-change on suspected primary failure).

### 2.6 Network Partitions and Split-Brain

A network partition occurs when the network splits into two or more disjoint subgroups of nodes such that nodes in different subgroups cannot communicate with each other, while communication within each subgroup may remain functional. This is distinct from node crashes: all nodes may be alive and correct, but connectivity is broken. A particularly dangerous consequence is split-brain, where multiple subgroups each believe they constitute the authoritative majority (or sole leader) and independently continue accepting writes or making leadership decisions, leading to divergent, conflicting system states that must later be reconciled (or that violate safety guarantees outright, e.g., two primaries accepting conflicting writes simultaneously). Quorum-based protocols (requiring a strict majority, e.g., more than n/2 nodes) are the standard mitigation, since at most one partition can contain a majority, preventing more than one side from making unilateral, conflicting progress.

### 2.7 Gray Failures and Partial Failures; Fail-Stop vs. Fail-Slow

Gray failures (a term popularized by Huang et al.) describe failures that are partial and inconsistently observed: a component is degraded or malfunctioning in a way that is not severe enough to trigger standard failure detectors or health checks, yet is severe enough to cause real user-visible impact — e.g., a server that responds to lightweight health-check pings correctly but is unable to serve a fraction of real requests due to resource exhaustion, a failing disk, or a stuck thread pool. The core problem with gray failures is a differential observability: different observers (a load balancer's health check vs. an application-level client) perceive the component's health differently, so no single vantage point reliably detects the degradation.

This motivates the fail-stop vs. fail-slow distinction: a fail-stop component ceases operation cleanly and (ideally) detectably, making failure handling comparatively tractable, whereas a fail-slow (or "limping but alive") component continues to operate but with degraded latency, throughput, or partial correctness, without crashing. Fail-slow failures are especially pernicious in large-scale systems because conventional failure detectors (built around binary alive/dead liveness checks) are poorly suited to detect them, and can require explicit latency- or quality-of-service-based anomaly detection instead.

### 2.8 Failure Detector Abstraction and Chandra-Toueg Classes

Because distinguishing "crashed" from "merely slow" is impossible in a purely asynchronous system (this impossibility underlies the FLP result that deterministic consensus is unsolvable in a fully asynchronous system with even one crash fault), Chandra and Toueg introduced the failure detector abstraction: an oracle, local to each process, that provides (possibly inaccurate) hints about which other processes have crashed. Failure detectors are classified along two axes — completeness (do crashed processes eventually get suspected by everyone?) and accuracy (are non-crashed processes ever wrongly suspected, and how does this change over time?):

- Strong completeness: every crashed process is eventually permanently suspected by every correct process.
- Weak completeness: every crashed process is eventually permanently suspected by some correct process.
- Strong accuracy: no correct process is ever suspected by any correct process, at any point.
- Weak accuracy: some correct process is never suspected by any correct process.
- Eventual strong accuracy: there is a point in time after which no correct process is suspected by any correct process (accuracy holds only eventually, allowing a period of unreliable suspicions beforehand).
- Eventual weak accuracy: there is a point in time after which some correct process is never again suspected.

Combining completeness and accuracy properties yields the named failure detector classes:

- Perfect failure detector (P): strong completeness + strong accuracy. Crashed processes are always eventually suspected, and no correct process is ever falsely suspected. This is the strongest class and is realistic only in synchronous systems with reliable timeout bounds.
- Strong failure detector (S): strong completeness + weak accuracy. All crashed processes are eventually suspected by everyone, but false suspicions of correct processes are permitted, as long as at least one correct process is never suspected.
- Eventually Perfect failure detector (◇P): strong completeness + eventual strong accuracy. Initially there may be false suspicions, but eventually the detector stabilizes such that crashes are always correctly identified and no correct process is suspected thereafter. This is the standard assumption underlying most practical partially synchronous consensus algorithms.
- Eventually Strong failure detector (◇S): strong completeness + eventual weak accuracy. This is the weakest class shown to be sufficient to solve consensus in an asynchronous system with crash faults, and it is of particular theoretical importance because Chandra and Toueg showed ◇S is sufficient, and Chandra, Hadzilacos, and Toueg later showed that ◇W (a related weak-completeness, eventual-weak-accuracy class) captures the weakest failure detector information necessary, making ◇S essentially the minimal useful class for solving consensus despite crash failures when f < n (a majority of correct processes is typically additionally required, e.g., for asynchronous consensus with crash faults, n > 2f).

The significance of this hierarchy is that it precisely delineates the boundary of solvability for consensus (and related problems like atomic broadcast, which is equivalent to consensus) in asynchronous systems augmented with failure detectors: FLP shows consensus is unsolvable with no failure detector information at all in a purely asynchronous system with even one crash fault, while Chandra-Toueg show that augmenting the system with a failure detector no stronger than ◇S (plus a majority of correct processes) is both necessary and sufficient to circumvent FLP and solve consensus deterministically. This makes ◇S the weakest failure detector for solving consensus under crash faults, and the P/◇P/S/◇S hierarchy provides the standard vocabulary for characterizing exactly how much synchrony or timing information a given real-world system (and its timeout-based failure detection implementation) effectively provides.
